items.prose: Packing a sixty-gallon oak leaching cask with sifted hardwood ashes over a tiered filter bed of rye straw and river pebbles allowed boiling rainwater to percolate slowly. The amber potash liquor drained through the bottom spigot with high potassium carbonate purity.

Testing lye strength using a fresh poultry egg confirmed optimal concentration when the egg floated buoyantly with a quarter-sized crown exposed above the surface. The traditional buoyancy benchmark indicated a specific gravity of 1.16.

Stirring fifty kilograms of freshly slaked quicklime into boiling potassium carbonate liquor precipitated insoluble calcium carbonate chalk. The causticizing reaction converted weak carbonate solution into aggressive, clear potassium hydroxide lye.

Passing raw caustic liquor through double-layered pressed wool felt pads stripped out microscopic carbon soot and colloidal clay. The clarified, sparkling straw-colored lye eliminated grey streaks in finished toilet soap batches.

A ruptured leaching hose splashed boiling 25° Bé caustic lye across an apprentice's forearm. Emergency dousing with 5% wood vinegar neutralized the slippery alkali within eight seconds, preventing irreversible third-degree chemical burns.

A calibrated glass Baumé hydrometer spindle floating in 20°C settled lye registered exactly 24.0° Bé. The verified density guaranteed stoichiometric saponification balance when paired with rendered mutton tallow charges.

Leaching ashes from boiler scrap pine introduced high concentrations of soluble sodium silicates and sticky abietic resin acids. The resulting lye produced a gummy, cloudy curd that refused to salt out cleanly.

Boiling down 600 liters of weak 10° Bé percolate in a massive hemispherical cast-iron kettle evaporated 400 liters of excess water. The concentrated 26.5° Bé heavy lye cut saponification cooking time from twelve hours to ninety minutes.
